tldr: Everyone you could call right now works in speech, which is why nobody in your network can refer you yet. Start with the few people you already know outside the field, then find the ones who hold your target title in three places: the subreddit for that job, the professional community that serves it, and the companies on your list.

blocks.text: You already do the hard part of networking every day. You meet a stranger, build rapport in ten minutes, gather background and plan the next steps, and you do it with a four-year-old, a nurse and a grandmother before lunch. What you are short of is people who work somewhere else, because years inside one profession fill a contact list with SLPs.
Start with the people you already know outside speech

A referral from someone who can vouch for you as a person carries more than any message to a stranger, so list these people before you write to anyone new. The ask is small and specific, and it never asks for a job.

items.title: Your grad cohort
items.text: Cohorts are small and stay findable. Search the program name on LinkedIn and read where people went: health tech, ed tech, device companies, pharma.

items.title: The reps in your building
items.text: The AAC device rep, the EMR trainer who ran your go-live, the ed-tech rep who sold to your district. They hold jobs on your map and already know you.

items.title: Colleagues who already left
items.text: The CF you supervised who never came back, the colleague who went to a vendor, your own CF supervisor. They are the warmest cold message you will send.

items.title: People outside healthcare
items.text: Your realtor, your insurance agent, anyone you worked with before grad school. They talk to everyone, and some never knew you as an SLP.

blocks.title: The warm ask
blocks.text:
I'm looking at [target title] roles, and I know you've been at [company] a while. Could you tell me what the [title] there actually does day to day? And if there's someone doing it you'd trust me to talk to, I'd love fifteen minutes with them.

No job ask. I'm working out whether it fits before I go further.

Say the title, because people do not guess on your behalf. If you have not decided between two titles, say both and stop there. When someone can't help, ask who else they know who works somewhere interesting, since that second name is often the one that matters.

blocks.title: Give them a title to remember

left.label: Forgettable
items: "Anything outside the clinic."
"Something non-clinical. I'm open."

right.label: Easy to repeat
items: "Clinical liaison roles."
"Clinical liaison or customer success. I'm working out which."

blocks.text: Ask a follow-up when someone tells you what they do

The person across the table at a barbecue is a free informational interview about a company you have never heard of. Ask three of these questions and you know whether the job exists at a company that would want a clinician, which is more than a posting tells you.

blocks.title: Seven follow-ups to "What do you do for work?"
blocks.text:
The company: What is it called, and who would I know that competes with it?
The structure: Who do you report to, and does anyone report to you?
The clients: Does the company have customers, and who are they?
The role: What is your title, and has it changed since you started?
The tools: What software is open on your screen most of the day?
The output: What do you hand over at the end of a week?
The style: Is the work mostly with other people, or mostly alone?
Have sixty seconds ready for "what are you looking for?"
Somewhere in the fifteen minutes they will ask, and your answer has four parts. Fill the brackets in yours tonight and say it out loud twice, so the first time you say it is before the call.

items.label: Your years
items.note: how long, and in which setting

items.label: What you'd keep
items.note: the two things you'd do all day

items.label: The title
items.note: the role you are moving into

items.label: The ask
items.note: who or what you'd like to hear about

blocks.title: Sixty seconds, out loud
blocks.note: Your path opens first. The chips show the others. The second sentence, the two things you'd do all day, is where what people said you were good at in lesson 1.4 belongs.

items.liaison-ur:
I've spent [N] years as a medical SLP, most of it in [acute / inpatient rehab / SNF], where half my week was case conferences, discharge planning and explaining to families and physicians why a patient did or didn't qualify for the next level of care. I'm moving into clinical liaison work, where that's the whole job. If you know a rehab facility or home health agency that's adding a liaison, I'd like to hear about it.

For utilization review instead:

[N] years as an SLP, and the part I'm good at is the part most people hate: reading the chart, matching what was done against what the payer will cover, and writing the justification that survives an audit. I'm moving into utilization review. If you know a health plan or a UR vendor that hires therapists into reviewer roles, I'd welcome an introduction.
items.customer-success: I'm an SLP with [N] years in [setting]. The part of the job I'd keep is onboarding: getting a family or a teacher to actually use the device or the plan after I leave the room. I'm moving into customer success at a health-tech or teletherapy company, where that's the work all day. If your team is hiring an implementation or onboarding specialist, I'd like to talk.
items.informatics: I've been the SLP who ends up fixing the documentation system. [N] years in [setting], superuser through the [EMR name] rollout, built the note templates the department still uses. I'm moving into clinical informatics, the analyst or trainer side, where I translate between the clinicians and the people building the system. If your organisation has an EHR analyst or trainer opening, I'd like to be considered.
items.clinical-educator: [N] years as an SLP, and the work I loved most was teaching other clinicians to use [AAC / a speaking valve / a dysphagia protocol]. I've trained [teams / a district / nursing staff] on it. I'm moving into a clinical educator role at a company that makes the products, where teaching clinicians is the job. If you know one that's hiring, I'd like to talk.
items.instructional-design: I'm an SLP with [N] years in [setting]. I've built training for adults the whole time: in-services, onboarding for CFs, a [program] the department still runs. I've rebuilt one of them as a [Rise / Storyline] module so you can see how I work. I'm moving into instructional design. If your team needs someone who can design for adults who are busy and sceptical, I'd like to show you the module.
items.data-analysis: [N] years as an SLP, and I'm the one who kept the outcome data nobody asked for: [dismissal rates / wait times / goal attainment] by [setting], in a spreadsheet that answered questions a year later. I'm moving into healthcare analytics, and I've been learning [SQL / Tableau] to do it properly. If your quality or analytics team has an analyst opening, I'd welcome a conversation.
items.project-management: For [N] years I've run programs that had a deadline, a budget and a dozen people who didn't report to me: [a caseload of 60 across three buildings / a dysphagia program / an EMR transition]. I'm moving into project management in healthcare, and I'm working through [the Google PM certificate / CAPM]. If your organisation has a coordinator or associate PM role, I'd like to be considered.
items.content-marketing: I'm an SLP with [N] years of explaining hard clinical ideas to people who didn't ask for a glossary: families, teachers, nurses. I've started writing that down: [a blog / three samples / a newsletter]. I'm moving into health content and marketing, where translation is the whole job. If your team needs a writer who has actually done the clinical work, I'd like to send you the samples.
items.sales-bd: [N] years as an SLP. Every week I sold a treatment plan to a family that didn't want to hear it and a protocol to nurses who were too busy for it, and most of them came round. I'm moving into clinical sales for a [device / health-tech] company, where that's the work with a quota attached. If your sales team is adding a clinical specialist, I'd like to hear about it.
items.research-coordinator: [N] years as an SLP in [setting], and the part of my week that ran most like a study was the part I ran best: consenting families, following the protocol to the letter, keeping the data clean and the follow-ups on schedule. I'm moving into clinical research coordination. If your site or sponsor has a coordinator opening, I'd like to be considered.
items.leadership: I've been an SLP in [setting] for [N] years and I already run the parts of the department nobody bills for: the schedule, the coverage, the audits, the new grad who's drowning. I'm looking to move into a clinical manager or program manager role, here or somewhere like here. Who did the last two openings go to, and what did they have that I don't yet?

blocks.text: List the companies whose products you already use

Write down every company whose product you use at work: the EMR, the AAC vendors, the teletherapy platform, the assessment publishers, the materials catalogue, the district's documentation system. Each of them needs people who can explain the clinical side to the teams building and selling the product, and you already know that product as a user. Their employees are your first cold list, and "I've used your product with [N] clients" is an opener few other applicants can write.
Request to join the closed Facebook groups today
SLPs who already got out keep naming private Facebook groups as the place that helped them.
The teacher transitioning groups on facebook are better. That's how I got out.

Groups like SLP alternatives and job transitions, Alternative Careers for Introverted SLPs, and the teacher-transition groups are closed and not indexed by search, so you cannot read them from outside. Request to join today, because approval can take days and waiting costs you nothing. Read a group for a week before you post, and when you do post, ask a question, which gives someone an easy reason to reply.
Find the people who hold your target title in three places

Search in the order industry, company, person, posting. Typing "non-clinical SLP" into a job board comes up empty, because a company writes its posting for a customer success manager and never for a clinician. Pick the industry, list the companies in it, find the people who hold the title there, and the postings follow.

items.label: Industry
items.note: health tech, ed tech or devices

items.label: Posting
items.note: last, once you know a name

items: Read the subreddit for the job title, not for your profession. Search Reddit for your target title and start with the complaint threads, where people describe the daily work in a way no posting will.

Find the professional community for that field: HIMSS and AMIA for informatics, your local PMI chapter for project management. For any other title, search the title plus "association" or "community". Many publish free articles and webinars.
Work through the companies on your list (linked under this lesson). They are health and ed-tech companies that value clinical skills, and every one of them has people on LinkedIn.

blocks.text: On LinkedIn, search People rather than posts. Put a company from your list in the Current company filter and speech-language pathologist or CCC-SLP in the keyword box. The search returns people who did your job and now work at that company, and their titles show you which jobs there a clinician holds.
At a conference, walk the exhibit hall

Most SLPs go to one conference a year, and it is full of SLPs. The exhibit hall is the exception: the companies on your list stand behind tables with people from their clinical teams, and few attendees walk up to ask about working there. The rooms for each path are smaller and further from home: HIMSS and AMIA for informatics, ATIA and Closing the Gap for AAC and assistive technology, DevLearn for instructional design, ISTELive for ed tech, and the local chapters of HIMSS and PMI, which cost far less.

items: Walk up to whoever is standing alone. They are relieved.
Change tables between sessions if yours has closed ranks.
Ask the organiser to introduce you, and say plainly that you are new to the field and want to meet people in it.
Say your sixty seconds, then hand the conversation back with a question about their work.
Close with "can I follow up on LinkedIn?" and do it that night.

blocks.title: The wrong room
blocks.text: The university's "alternative careers for SLPs" panel and the SLP career fair are full of people in exactly your position. Good for morale, useless for leads. Spend the evening in a room where people already have the job.
Save three names before you write a single message
Save the names as you find them on your people and applications page (linked under this lesson). Lesson 3.3 sends from the same list and lesson 3.6 keeps it warm, so a name goes in once.

items.q: At a barbecue, your neighbour says she works "in software, sort of". What do you do next?
options: Nod and move on, since she isn't in healthcare.
Ask what the company is called, who its customers are and what her title is.
Ask whether her company is hiring.
items.why: Three follow-ups tell you whether the job exists at a company that would want a clinician, and a hiring question gives her nothing she can answer.

items.q: A former colleague asks what kind of job you want. You are torn between clinical liaison and customer success. What do you say?
options: "I'm not sure yet. I'll tell you when I've decided."
"Anything outside the clinic, honestly."
"Clinical liaison or customer success, and I'm working out which."
items.why: Two titles give her two things to remember and pass on, and "anything" gives her nothing.

items: Request to join two closed groups today and forget about them until they let you in.
Find the subreddit for your target title and read the top posts of the month.
Run one LinkedIn people search: a company from your list, plus CCC-SLP.
Save three names in the tracker. You will message them in lesson 3.3.

takeaways: Everyone you could call works in speech, so start with the few who don't: your grad cohort, the reps in your building and the colleagues who already left.
Say the title you want. "Anything outside the clinic" gives people nothing to remember you by.
Have sixty seconds ready for "what are you looking for?": your years, the two things you'd do all day, the title, the ask.
Search in the order industry, company, person, posting. A LinkedIn people search for a company on your list plus CCC-SLP finds SLPs who already work there.
Request to join two closed Facebook groups today, and save three names before you write a single message.

tldr: The message that gets answered is short, names the move they made, and asks for fifteen minutes about their path with no job attached. On a free LinkedIn account you connect first with a note under 200 characters, then send the full message. Roughly one ask in four gets no reply, which is a volume problem rather than a verdict, so you follow up once and stop.

blocks.text: Referrals decide most of the documented transitions, and generic applications through Indeed and LinkedIn without one are what fails. The ask that starts a referral is small: fifteen minutes, about how they got in, with no job attached.
Did you find the new position through network connections or just by submitting your resume?

Readers of the exit posts already suspect that referrals matter. Under one post, more than twenty people asked the writer for their actual résumé, which is a far bigger ask than fifteen minutes about how one person got in.
Make your first message easy to answer

A stranger answers when the message is plainly written to them and a yes costs thirty seconds. Most people leave out the easy way to decline, and that line is what makes a stranger feel safe replying at all.

items.title: Name the move they made
items.text: One specific thing shows you are writing to them and not to forty people.

items.title: Ask for fifteen minutes
items.text: A fixed, small amount of time, with two time windows or a booking link, so a yes needs no calendar negotiation.

items.title: Attach no job ask
items.text: No résumé and no "are you hiring?". Ask one direct question they could answer in a sentence.

items.title: Make it easy to decline
items.text: Offer a one-question fallback by message in case a call is too much.

blocks.title: The message that doesn't get answered, and the one that does
blocks.before: Hi! I'm a speech pathologist looking to leave the field. I saw you're a Customer Success Manager. Could you tell me what a typical project looks like from start to finish, how you got the job, what the interview was like, what the salary is, and whether they're hiring? Also, would you be willing to look at my résumé?
blocks.after: Hi [Name], I'm an SLP in [setting] looking at implementation roles, and you made exactly that move. Would you have fifteen minutes in the next couple of weeks? I mostly want to know how you got the first one. No job ask, I promise.

blocks.text: The first message asks a stranger for two hours of work, attaches a résumé, and never says which title it means. The second asks for one thing. If Google could answer a question, don't ask a person.
On LinkedIn, connect first and send the full message second

A free LinkedIn account can only message people you are connected to, so a stranger gets a connection request first. The note on that request is capped at 200 characters on a free account, and LinkedIn allows only a few notes a month, so save them for the people you most want to reach. When the notes run out, send the request bare. Either way, send the full message once they accept, or by email if you can find an address. Some people will not accept, and the ones who do now recognise your name.

items.label: Full message
items.note: once they accept, or by email

blocks.title: The connection request, under 200 characters once you fill it in
blocks.text:
Hi [Name], I'm an SLP looking at [target title] roles, and I saw you made that move from [their old setting]. I'd be glad to connect. I have one question about your first year, if you're open.

If you share a program:

Hi [Name], I saw you went through [program] too and you're now at [company]. I'm an SLP looking at [target title] roles and would love to connect and ask how you got there.

Keep the full message between 50 and 125 words. Emails of that length got the best response rates in one company's analysis of its own data (Boomerang, 2016), and one to three questions did better than none or many.

blocks.title: The first message (email, or LinkedIn once you are connected), 50 to 125 words
blocks.text:
Hi [Name], I'm an SLP in [setting] and I'm looking at [target title] roles. You made the same move, and I'd rather ask you than read another article about it.

Would you be up for 15 minutes in the next couple of weeks? I'm free [two windows, e.g. Tuesday after 4 or Thursday lunchtime], or here's a link if that's easier: [booking link]. I mostly want to know how you got the first one and what you'd do differently. No job ask, I promise.

If a call is too much, one question by message would still help me: [the one thing you most want to know].

Either way, thank you for putting your path somewhere I could find it.

[Your name]
Follow up once, then stop

Send one follow-up seven to ten days later. Silence usually means a full inbox and a bad Tuesday. A second follow-up reads as pressure, and it costs you the chance to write again in six months, when you have something new to say.

blocks.title: The follow-up, once, seven to ten days later
blocks.text:
Hi [Name], floating this back up in case it got buried.

Still would love 15 minutes on how you got into [target title]. If a call is too much, I'd happily take two sentences by message instead: what surprised you most in your first three months?

Thank you either way. [Your name]
Bring these six questions to the call

blocks.title: Six questions for the fifteen minutes
blocks.text:
1. What did you actually do yesterday?
2. What did your employer require, and what did they ignore on your résumé?
3. Which part of clinical work turned out to be the most useful, and which part did you have to unlearn?
4. Which groups, newsletters or communities should I be in?
5. What would you do differently if you were starting this month?
6. Who else should I be talking to?

Never skip the last question, because "who else should I be talking to?" is the one that turns a conversation into an introduction. The first asks for the day rather than the job description, and the fourth turns a fifteen-minute call into a channel that keeps sending you things.
Thank them the same day, then tell them what you did

blocks.title: The thank-you, same day
blocks.text:
[Name], thank you for the time. The thing I'm taking away is [one specific sentence they said, in their words].

I'm going to [the one concrete thing you'll do because of it] in the next two weeks, and I'll let you know how it lands. If [person they mentioned] would be open to the same 15 minutes, I'd be grateful for an introduction whenever it's convenient.

And if there's anything you're working on that a clinician could help with, or anyone you'd like an introduction to, say the word.

Thank you again. [Your name]

Send the thank-you the same day, do the thing you said you would do, and tell them two weeks later that you did it. In one experiment, 66% of helpers who were thanked helped again, against 32% of those who got a neutral reply (Grant & Gino, 2010, a lab scenario with students). The offer at the end can be small: a clinician's read on a product, a name from your own department, a share of something they wrote.

items.q: Ten days after your first message, there is still no reply. What do you do?
options: Message again every few days until they answer.
Assume the answer is no and cross their company off your list.
Send one follow-up with a one-question fallback, then stop.
items.why: Silence usually means a full inbox, one follow-up is polite, and a second costs you the chance to write again in six months.

items.q: You found an SLP who became an implementation manager. You are not connected, and your LinkedIn account is free. What do you send first?
options: A connection request with a short note that names her move and offers one question.
Your résumé and five questions about the job.
Nothing. Apply to her company and hope she notices.
items.why: A free account can only message connections, and a note that names her move gives her a reason to accept.

items: Fill your setting, your target title and your name into the connection request, the first message and the follow-up tonight.
Run the first message through the checklist above.
Leave the [Name] blanks empty. You fill them in lesson 3.3.

takeaways: Referrals decide most documented transitions, and applications sent without one are what fails.
Ask for fifteen minutes about their path, with no job attached and an easy way to decline.
On a free LinkedIn account, send a connection request with a note under 200 characters, then the full message once they accept.
Follow up once, seven to ten days later, then stop.
"Who else should I be talking to?" is the question that turns a conversation into an introduction.

tldr: Send three messages in twenty minutes, tonight. Roughly one ask in four gets no answer, so sending three keeps a single silence from reading as a verdict, and one conversation is worth more than another week of reading.

blocks.text: This is the step people postpone for months and call research. You already know enough to send three messages, and they do not all have to go to strangers.
Pick three people, in this order of value

items.title: An SLP with your title
items.text: They have already done the exact translation you are attempting.

items.title: Anyone who holds that title
items.text: Whatever their background, they know what their employer actually required.

items.title: Someone at a target company
items.text: A name inside beats a posting outside. The list from lesson 3.1 holds health and ed-tech companies that value clinical skills.

blocks.title: Choose the person most likely to answer

left.label: Skip
items: The SLP with the big account and a course, who gets a pile of messages like yours.
Someone a few months into the role.

right.label: Prefer
items: The SLP who quietly became an EHR analyst and rarely gets asked.
Someone who has held the title for years, ideally at more than one company.

blocks.text: Send three so that one silence means nothing

Three is a volume decision. Between one in five and one in four of these asks gets no answer at all, so a single message can land in a full inbox and feel like a verdict on you. People also say yes more often than askers predict: in one set of studies, askers underestimated by as much as 50% how likely others were to agree to a direct request (Flynn & Lake, 2008). Send them tonight, with the templates already filled in, because a tired brain will not do this on a Thursday three weeks from now.
burnt out brains really struggle to use executive functions, so planning and executing a career change is gonna be hard
blocks.from: an SLP, quoted in the research file

blocks.text: Expect an ordinary Tuesday, a second name or an unlisted posting

What comes back is rarely a job. You get a description of an ordinary Tuesday, the credential their employer actually cared about, a posting that is not public yet, or a second name. The conversations are also interview prep, because you arrive at the interview using the words people in the role use. And they narrow your map: if after a few calls you have gone quiet on one path and keep asking about another, cross the first one off.

blocks.title: Do not ask for a job in the first message
blocks.text: The ask is fifteen minutes about their path. A job ask puts a stranger in the position of saying no to something they cannot give you, and a message they cannot say yes to is easy to leave unanswered. The referral comes later, at the end of a good conversation, when you ask who else you should be talking to.

items.q: You have time for one message tonight. Which of these three people gets it?
options: An SLP with a large following who sells a career-change course.
An SLP who became an EHR analyst four years ago and rarely posts.
A customer success manager who started the job two months ago.
items.why: The analyst has done your exact translation, has held the title for years, and gets far fewer messages than the visible account.

items.q: Your draft ends with "and if your team is hiring, I'd love to be considered." What do you do before you send it?
options: Leave it in, because it shows you are serious.
Move it to the first line so they see it.
Cut it, and ask only for fifteen minutes about their path.
items.why: A job ask makes a stranger say no to something they cannot give you, and the referral comes later, when you ask who else to talk to.

blocks.text: Send all three before the timer runs out

items: Set a timer for twenty minutes.
Open the three names you saved in lesson 3.1.

Paste the first-message template, or the connection-request note for anyone you are not connected to on LinkedIn. Change the name, the setting and the target title, and read it once for anything that sounds like a cover letter.
Send all three before the timer runs out.
Log them in the tracker with today's date, and set a reminder eight days out for the single follow-up.

action.label: I sent three
action.prompt: Fill in the first-message template for three people: an SLP who now holds your target title, anyone else with that title, and someone at a company on your list. Change the name, the setting and the target role in each one. Send all three tonight, log them in the tracker with today's date, and set a reminder eight days out for the single follow-up.
action.done: Three sent. Expect one silence, and that is the math working rather than anything about you.

takeaways: Message three people tonight: an SLP with your target title, anyone with that title, and someone at a company on your list.
Three is a volume decision. Roughly one ask in four gets no reply, and three sent keeps one silence from reading as a verdict.
Prefer people who have held the title for years, and skip the account with the big following.
Never ask for a job in the first message. Ask for fifteen minutes about how they got where they are.
What comes back is a real Tuesday, a credential that mattered, an unlisted posting, or a second name.

tldr: Recruiters look you up before they call, and they find you in the first place by searching the words in the job they are filling. Put those words in your headline and skills, keep the clinical history, and write to a hiring manager or in-house recruiter when a role is live: follow up once at eight days, then stop.

blocks.text: A recruiter who likes your translated résumé looks you up before reaching out. If they find a headline that says Speech-Language Pathologist, CCC-SLP, an About section about your passion for pediatric feeding and a skills list topped by Dysphagia, the two documents describe different people, and the recruiter believes the profile.
Put the words a recruiter searches on your profile

Recruiters search the vocabulary of the role they are filling, so a profile written only in clinical terms never appears in their results. From the inside, that feels identical to being turned down. Put your path's terms in the headline, About, job descriptions and skills.

blocks.title: Search terms for your profile
blocks.note: Your path opens first. List a tool or certificate only once it is true of you.

blocks.title: What a recruiter reads in a headline

left.label: Reads as undecided
items: "Transitioning SLP"
"Burnt-out SLP seeking non-clinical roles"
"Aspiring instructional designer"
Four unrelated titles separated by bars

right.label: Reads as decided
items: The target title first
One line of clinical credibility with a number
CCC-SLP last, as an asset

blocks.text: Pick one target, or two that belong together, and let the rest of the map wait.

blocks.title: Before you touch the profile
blocks.text: Turn off "Share profile updates" (Settings & Privacy, then Visibility, under Visibility of your LinkedIn activity). On some screens the same switch is labelled "Share job changes, education changes, and work anniversaries from profile". Left on, LinkedIn can announce a profile edit to your connections, and in a department of six people that includes your lead. Edit from a personal laptop on a personal email, never the district one. You are allowed a LinkedIn: plenty of your colleagues have one, and a profile is not a resignation.
Fix the rest of the profile in this order

items: Rewrite the headline: target-role words first, one line of bridge credibility with a number, credential last. It takes ten minutes, and the headline shows on every comment and connection request you make.
Reorder your skills so the target-role terms sit at the top and the clinical ones further down (in the Skills section, open the edit menu and choose Reorder).
Rewrite About as three short first-person paragraphs: the bridge claim with a number, two translated accomplishments, then where you are heading and what you have already done to get ready.
Translate the top three bullets under each recent role so each says how big it was, what you did and what changed, and leave the rest alone. Lesson 4.2 goes through the method.
Set Open to Work to "Recruiters only" and type in your target titles. LinkedIn tries to hide this from recruiters at your own employer and says it cannot guarantee that.

Search LinkedIn for your target title plus CCC-SLP and write down three people who have already made this move. Then open ten profiles of people who hold the title and read only their certifications: whatever appears on seven is worth having, and whatever appears on one is what somebody sold them.
Follow five companies from your list and join one group for the field, so the feed shows you their openings and their people instead of the caseload discourse.

blocks.title: Do not scrub the clinician out
blocks.text: A profile with a hole where a decade should be raises more questions than a translated one, and at speech-tech companies the license is the qualification. Never change a title, a date or a role to something it was not. Fabrication is the one screening flag nobody recovers from, and your résumé and profile will be read side by side.

blocks.title: Everything you post sits under your name
blocks.text: A recruiter who finds you can read your recent posts and comments on your profile. A post about the caseload, a reply venting about administration, a like on someone else's exit rant: each one answers the retention question for them before you get to. Use LinkedIn the way you'd speak in a conference room with the hiring manager in it, and keep the venting for the closed groups.

If you are aiming at content, instructional design or clinical education, post one or two plain pieces about something you know cold, such as how dysphagia documentation gets written on a unit, or what makes an AAC rollout stick after the SLP leaves. Post nothing for engagement, and nothing you would not want a hiring manager to read first.
Answer in-house recruiters, and ignore the staffing agencies
The recruiters SLPs warn each other about work for clinical staffing and contract agencies, whose business is placing clinicians into caseloads at a margin.
No recruiters ever. Never ever.

An in-house recruiter at a health-tech company does a different job. They have a role to fill this quarter, and a candidate who clearly fits is the most useful thing that can land in their inbox. One documented transition happened that way: a recruiter found a self-taught SLP on LinkedIn, and she ended up at $93,000 as a software engineer.

left.label: Skip it
items: A cold "keep me in mind" note. With no role attached, they have nothing to act on.
Any recruiter who answers "I want out of clinical work" with three SNF contracts.

right.label: Send it
items: There is a live posting and you match most of its requirement lines.
Your first line names the target title.
You name the clinical background as an asset, without apologising for it.

blocks.text: Some recruiters place only into health IT, only into device companies' clinical teams, or only into learning and development. Connecting with two of them now, without a pitch, costs nothing and means they can find you before you need them.
When a role is live, write to the person who hires for it
The person who decides is usually findable on LinkedIn, and the note needs one line of proof and one ask.

blocks.title: The note to a hiring manager when a role is live
blocks.text:
Hi [Name], does the [title] role posted on [LinkedIn / your careers page] report to you? I've spent [N] years as an SLP in [setting], and [one specific, verifiable thing: trained fourteen clinicians through an EMR rollout / ran a caseload of 62 across three sites / built the dysphagia protocol the unit still uses]. I've applied. If you're the person hiring for it, I'd like the chance to talk.

[Your name]
If a recruiter says you're not qualified, treat it as the start of a conversation. Name the gap, say what you'd do about it by the interview date, and ask a question they can say yes to.

blocks.title: When a recruiter says you're not qualified
blocks.text:
Thanks for being straight with me. I don't have [Salesforce / Articulate / SQL] yet. If I complete [a named course] before the interview date, would you be comfortable putting me forward? My [N] years in [setting] cover [the two requirements you do meet], and I learn tools fast because I've had to.

If the answer is still no, I'd value one line on what would change it, and when it's reasonable to check back.
Follow up once at eight days, and add something new

Send one follow-up eight days after the first message, and make it add something: a line about what you built, or a specific question about the role. End by asking whether the role is still open, which is easy to answer and tells you whether to keep going. Then stop. Roles get frozen and pipelines fill before anyone updates a posting, so silence from a recruiter is about the role far more often than it is about you.

blocks.title: The eight-day follow-up
blocks.text: Hi [name], following up on [role] from last week. Since I wrote, I put together [the artifact, in six words] which is close to what the posting describes under [requirement line]. Happy to send it over if it is useful. Either way, is the role still open?

items.q: You are about to rewrite your headline, and your department lead is one of your LinkedIn connections. What do you do first?
options: Rewrite it tonight and hope nobody notices.
Turn off "Share profile updates" in Settings, then edit.
Delete your SLP jobs so the new profile looks complete.
items.why: That switch is what announces profile edits to your connections, and deleting clinical history leaves a hole that raises more questions than a translated one.

items.q: A health-tech company you like has no open role that fits you. You find one of its recruiters on LinkedIn. What do you send?
options: Nothing yet. Follow the company, and write when a role you match is posted.
A note asking them to keep you in mind.
Your résumé, in case something opens.
items.why: With no live role there is nothing for a recruiter to act on, and a note about a posting you match gives them something to do with you.

items: Open the tracker and find anyone you messaged eight or more days ago.
Send one follow-up each, adding one new thing.
Mark them closed. No third message.

takeaways: Your profile does two jobs: it corroborates the résumé, and it is how recruiters find you in the first place.
Recruiters search the vocabulary of the role, so put those words in your headline, About, job descriptions and skills.
Turn off "Share profile updates" before you edit, and set Open to Work to "Recruiters only".
Translate the history and never delete or relabel it. At speech-tech companies the clinical credential is the asset.
Message a recruiter or hiring manager only about a live role, and follow up once at eight days with something new.

tldr: One documented search took more than 500 applications in six months, and referrals decide most successful transitions. Look for someone inside before you apply, and keep two conversations warm with one short update a month, so that a referral gets offered before you have to ask for it.

blocks.text: You can be the best of two hundred and forty-two strangers, or you can be the person somebody already mentioned. Referrals decide most of the documented transitions.

items.label: applications over six months, one documented analyst transition
applicants per opening on average, up 111% since 2022
roughly, how many informational-interview asks get no answer
the window in which an application is most likely to be seen

blocks.text: The 500 belongs to an SLP who landed a fully remote analyst role paying $20,000 more than their best year in the clinic. Cold applications worked for that search, and 500 was the price.
Do these four things every time you apply

items: **Apply inside 48 hours.** Postings get most of their real attention in the first day or two. A tailored application on day one beats a perfect one on day nine.

**Check for an in before you hit submit.** Search the company on LinkedIn for anyone from your program, anyone with CCC-SLP in their history, anyone you have ever met. If one exists, message them first and apply second. If none exists, apply anyway and note it in the tracker.

**Message one person at the company the same day.** Pick someone doing the job you applied for, ideally a former clinician, or the hiring manager (that note is in lesson 3.4). Say you applied, name the one specific thing that made you want the role, and ask one question.
**Turn every conversation into a name.** At the end of any informational interview, ask who else they would talk to if they were you. A network grows from that question.

blocks.text: Ask for the referral after the conversation, never in the first message

Ask for fifteen minutes about their work first, because referrals come at the end of a conversation that already happened, and most are offered before you request them. Referring you means putting their own name behind your work, and few people do that for someone they have never spoken to. After a real conversation the bet changes, and many companies pay an employee a bonus when someone they referred gets hired. A referral can also get a résumé read when it sits a little under the posted requirements.

blocks.title: After a good conversation
blocks.text: This was genuinely useful, thank you. Two things before I let you go. Is there anyone else you'd talk to if you were me? And if a [role] opens on your team, would you be open to me sending you the posting?

The second question is the referral ask in its least awkward form: a yes or no about a hypothetical, and it gives you permission to come back. Ask one more near the end: what other companies do work like yours? Write every name on your people and applications page, with the person they suggested next in its own column.
Keep two conversations warm, and keep sending new messages

You need two or three people who know what you are looking for and would forward you a posting, which is a much smaller job than building a network. Two warm conversations is the floor you keep, and new messages replace one when it goes quiet. The tracker counts your week and shows who is due, and lesson 3.8 shows how to hand the research and the first draft to an AI tool.

items.title: Every month
items.text: One four-sentence update to each of your two warm contacts.

blocks.title: One contact, from first message to referral

blocks.text: Send each person one update a month

One message a month, per person, reminds them you exist and shows that you did something since last time. The last sentence matters most, because remembering what they told you separates a relationship from a mailing list.

blocks.title: The monthly update
blocks.text: Hi [name], quick update since we talked. I [built the thing / finished the certificate / had a first interview at X]. Still aiming at [role type]. If anything crosses your desk I'd love to hear about it. Hope [specific thing they mentioned] went well.

Twice, the update becomes an ask. When the thing you build in lesson 5.2 exists, send it with "would you look at this and tell me what a hiring manager would say?", a small job that puts your work in front of the person most likely to pass it on. And the week you switch from building to applying, send the message below to everyone you have spoken to.

blocks.title: The week you start applying
blocks.text: Hi [name], I'm applying now, for [title] roles. If you hear of one, I'd be grateful for a nudge.

blocks.title: The useful introduction often comes from a loose tie
blocks.text: A randomised study of more than 20 million LinkedIn members found that moderately weak ties, people you share some mutual connections with, led to more job moves than close ties or near-strangers (Rajkumar et al., Science, 2022). A former SLP who answered you once is that kind of tie, and the most-engaged exit posts end with an offer to message the writer.
When someone goes quiet, follow up once and wait

They are busy, and the silence is not about you. Send one follow-up after two weeks, let it rest, and come back in six months with something new to say. After you land, a note twice a year to the people who helped keeps them from becoming strangers again, and they are your insurance if the new job turns out to be the wrong one.

items.q: A role you want was posted yesterday, and a classmate from your grad program works at the company. What do you do?
options: Spend a week perfecting the application, then apply.
Message the classmate today, then apply inside 48 hours.
Apply, then ask the recruiter to refer you.
items.why: An application gets most of its attention in the first two days, and someone inside who knows you is worth more than a perfect résumé on day nine.

items.q: A month ago you had a good fifteen-minute call with a customer success manager. What do you send her now?
options: A four-sentence update on what you did since, ending on something she mentioned.
Nothing, because you don't want to bother her.
A request to refer you for any open role.
items.why: One short update a month keeps the conversation warm, and referrals get offered at the end of a relationship that already exists.

action.label: Two are warm
action.prompt: Pick the two most promising people from your tracker and send each of them a monthly update this week. Four sentences, ninety seconds, ending with a question about something they told you.
action.done: Two warm. That is the network. It does not need to be bigger than this.

takeaways: Applying without referrals is the expensive route: one documented search took more than 500 applications.
Apply inside 48 hours, look for someone inside first, and message someone at the company the same day.
Never ask for a referral in a first message. Ask for fifteen minutes, then ask who else you should talk to.
Two live conversations is the floor, because you need a couple of people who would forward you a posting, and that is smaller than a network.
One four-sentence update a month keeps a conversation warm.

tldr: An AI chat tool such as ChatGPT or Claude is good at the parts of a search that are not you: research, first drafts, rehearsal, tidying notes. Hand those over, keep the specifics and the send, and never paste a client's details or an employer's document into it.

blocks.text: Most of the hours in a search go on work an AI chat tool does quickly and you do slowly: reading a stranger's profile for the one thing worth mentioning, working out what a company sells, turning a page of call notes into three facts and a task. The tool writes the draft and you write the sentence, because the detail that gets you hired was never in the tool to begin with. Lesson 4.1 applies the same rule to your résumé.
Hand over the reading and the first draft, and keep the specifics and the send

left.label: Hand over
items: Research: paste a profile or a careers page and ask what a clinician would notice.
The first draft of a message, a thank-you or an update.
Rehearsal: it plays the person you are about to call.
Tidying: notes into next steps, a posting into a checklist.

right.label: Keep
items: The specifics: the caseload that hit 62 in March, the fourteen people you trained.
The send: read every message out loud before it goes.
The judgement about who to write to and whether a reply was warm.
Anything private.

blocks.text: The first draft is where people stall for a week, so let the tool produce it and then rewrite it in your words. In rehearsal it will play the customer success lead who used to be an OT and interrupt you when you ask something you could have searched, at eleven at night when nobody else will. You can also ask it which conferences, groups and newsletters your target title reads, as long as you treat the answer as leads to verify, because it gets some names wrong.

Generic output erases the details that make you the one candidate with a story: the parent who said no for four months was never in the tool. If you would not say a sentence to the person's face at the copier, cut it. Deciding who to write to and who to leave alone is clinical judgement, and you already have it.

blocks.title: Never paste
blocks.text: A client's name or anything that could identify one, a session note, a chart, an IEP, an evaluation report, an internal email, your employer's templates or policies, or a screenshot of any of those. Protected health information does not stop being protected because you removed the name, and a personal ChatGPT or Claude account comes with no HIPAA agreement. Use a personal account on a personal laptop, the same rule as lesson 3.4, check the privacy settings for whether your chats train the tool, and assume anything you paste is kept.

blocks.title: It will invent
blocks.text: A conference that does not exist, a person's current title, a statistic with a confident decimal, a product the company never made. It is a drafting tool, not a source. Verify every name before you rely on it, and never let a number it produced into a message, a résumé or an interview answer.
Copy the prompts, already filled in with your details

Each prompt below carries your path and, if you mined them in lesson 4.3, your numbers. Add the company or the person and copy. Most of them ask the tool to interview you first, so the draft is built from your answers.
Send two messages a week while you build, and five once you apply

With the reading and the first draft handed over, a personalised message takes a fraction of the time it used to, and the limit on how many you send becomes your attention. Send two a week while you are building and five a week once you are applying. The tracker from lesson 3.6 counts the week and tells you who is due.

items.title: The tool reads
items.text: Profiles, careers pages and postings, and it writes the first draft.

items.title: The tracker remembers
items.text: Who you wrote to, when, and who is due a follow-up.

items.title: You talk
items.text: The rewrite, the send and the call are yours.

items.q: You want help turning an evaluation report you wrote into a résumé bullet. What do you paste into the AI tool?
options: The report, with the child's name removed.
Your own summary: how many evaluations a year, what you did, what changed. No client details.
A screenshot of the report instead of the text.
items.why: Health information stays protected after the name comes off, and your own numbers are all the tool needs.

items.q: The draft it gives you says you "improved outcomes by 34%". You never gave it that figure. What do you do?
options: Keep it, because it sounds about right.
Soften it to "about a third".
Delete it and use a number you can trace to your own work.
items.why: The tool invents numbers with a straight face, and none of its numbers belongs in a message, a résumé or an interview answer.

items: Pick one name from your people list who is still at "to message".
Run the research prompt on their profile and write down the one thing worth mentioning.
Run the interview-me prompt, answer its five questions honestly, and take the draft.
Rewrite it in your words, read it aloud, send it, and log "Sent the first message" in the tracker.

takeaways: Hand the AI tool the research, the first draft, the rehearsal and the tidying. Keep the specifics, the send and the judgement about people.
Never paste anything that identifies a client, or any document that belongs to your employer. Personal account, personal laptop.
It invents names and numbers with a straight face. Verify before you rely on it, and never let its numbers into a message or a résumé.
Ask it to interview you before it drafts. The answers are the material.
With the drafting handed over, two messages a week while building and five while applying is a real pace, and the tracker keeps the count.
